---
title: "Apptainer: Containerizing Your Analysis for Portability"
sidebar: arcs04
---

> **Part 4b of a 2-hour session.** Hour 1 ([DESeq2](07-deseq2.qmd)) built a
> working pipeline locally. This hour packages that same pipeline in an
> Apptainer container so it runs identically on any operating system. We work
> in GitHub Codespaces because Apptainer is Linux-only — Codespaces gives
> everyone an identical browser-based Linux environment in about two minutes.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this hour you will be able to:

- **Explain** how containerization addresses reproducibility problems caused by software and OS differences
- **Execute** the Part 4a DESeq2 pipeline from inside an Apptainer container
- **Differentiate** a host environment from a containerized environment, and identify when each is appropriate
- **Modify** a provided Apptainer definition and re-run the pipeline to confirm reproducible results

## Prerequisites

[Part 4a — DESeq2](07-deseq2.qmd). A GitHub account with Codespaces access.

---

## 1. The problem: "works on my machine"

<!-- Frame: your pipeline runs in Positron on your laptop. Your collaborator
     on Windows can't install half the Bioconductor dependencies. The OS,
     R version, and package versions all differ. Containers are how we make
     that problem go away. -->

## 2. Launch the Codespace

<!-- Click "Open in Codespace" on the workshop repo. The devcontainer.json
     pre-installs Apptainer and pulls a pre-built .sif image, so by the time
     the Codespace opens you're ready to run.

     Budget ~5 minutes here for the slowest launches. -->

Confirm the environment is ready:

```bash
apptainer --version
ls ~/images/deseq2.sif
```

## 3. Host vs. container — what just changed?

<!-- Same machine, two environments. Show R version on the host vs. inside
     the container. Talk through when each is appropriate: host for daily
     interactive work, container for "this must run identically elsewhere." -->

```bash
# Host R (whatever the Codespace ships with — may be absent)
R --version || echo "no R on the host"

# Container R (pinned by the .sif image)
apptainer exec ~/images/deseq2.sif R --version
```

## 4. Run the Part 4a pipeline from inside the container

<!-- Clone the learner's own Part 4a repo into the Codespace. Bind-mount
     the project directory into the container and run pipeline.R. Compare
     results/ to what they produced locally in hour 1 — they should match. -->

```bash
git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/arcs-part4.git
cd arcs-part4

apptainer exec --bind "$PWD":/work \
  ~/images/deseq2.sif \
  Rscript /work/scripts/pipeline.R
```

## 5. Read the container definition

<!-- Open container/deseq2.def. Walk through the sections: Bootstrap/From,
     %post (what gets installed), %environment, %runscript, %test.
     This is the file that *defines* the reproducible environment. -->

## 6. Modify the definition and re-run

<!-- The "Create"-level exercise. Pick ONE change:
       - Add a CRAN package to the %post block
       - Pin a different Bioconductor release in the From: line
     Rebuild the image (or pull the instructor's pre-built variant to save
     time), re-run the pipeline, confirm results are still reproducible. -->

## 7. Wrap-up: the repo is the reproducible artifact

<!-- Push the modified .def alongside the code. Anyone with the repo + a
     Linux machine (or a Codespace) can reproduce the analysis bit-for-bit.
     This is the end of the ARCS arc: reproducible code (Parts 1–2),
     reproducible data wrangling (Part 3a), reproducible history (Part 3b),
     reproducible environment (Part 4). -->

## Materials

The `devcontainer.json`, `setup.sh`, and `deseq2.def` used in this hour live
under `workshops/arcs_04/materials/` in the ARCS repo — use them as a starting
template for containerizing your own analyses.
